scores.reason: European consumer financial default experiments with effect sizes, plus direct evidence that defaults reduce perceived trustworthiness — hits C1, C4, C5 and feeds both the entry and level decisions.

Field experiment showing an enrolment-metric win with no underlying behaviour change at six months in a consumer credit product — the exact vanity-enrolment failure mode the brief asks to test (C2, C4), and it contradicts the premise.

Quantifies how preset menus anchor amounts and the welfare effect of changing the preset options in a consumer self-directed setting — directly informs the 1x/2x/5x versus blank-field decision (C3, C4, C5).

The strongest recent quantitative evidence that default-driven gains shrink over the medium run once opt-out and withdrawal are counted (C1, C2); employer setting, but the brief accepts that literature by analogy and this contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise.
Review framework for when default effects persist downstream — useful for the 6-12 month persistence question (C2), though it offers moderators rather than effect sizes.

EU legal taxonomy distinguishing acceptable defaults from dark patterns, including pre-selected options — directly relevant to the reputational/regulatory dimension of the entry decision (C5), though normative rather than empirical evidence.

Classic 401(k) automatic-enrolment evidence showing years-long anchoring at the default rate (C1, C2, C3); relevant by analogy but it is exactly the older employer-plan work the brief says matters less, and it is oddly placed as a scored rather than foundational packet.

Directly tests whether the level of a preset default anchors people at a rate they would not otherwise choose and finds low-income users anchor hardest — squarely C3 and C5, central to the multiplier decision despite the employer setting.

Foundational slot: canonical household-finance synthesis covering choice architecture in consumer (not just employer) settings — real background worth knowing, though not the single result the newer papers are arguing with.

Foundational slot: the clean randomized demonstration that a consumer-fintech nudge helps on average while harming a vulnerable subgroup — the exact distributional-risk result (C5) a newcomer needs before weighing the rest of this list.
